1: “I shall never, never believe,” Nastya prattled, “that the old women find babies among the cabbages in the kitchen-garden. It’s winter now and there are no cabbages, and so the old woman couldn’t have taken Katerina a daughter.”
3: “Or perhaps they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to those who are married.”
4: Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, pondering profoundly.
5: “Nastya, how silly you are!” he said at last, firmly and calmly. “How can Katerina have a baby when she isn’t married?”
7: “You know nothing about it,” she snapped irritably. “Perhaps she has a husband, only he is in prison, so now she’s got a baby.”
8: “But is her husband in prison?” the matter-of-fact Kostya inquired gravely.
9: “Or, I tell you what,” Nastya interrupted impulsively, completely rejecting and forgetting her first hypothesis. “She hasn’t a husband, you are right there, but she wants to be married, and so she’s been thinking of getting married, and thinking and thinking of it till now she’s got it, that is, not a husband but a baby.”
10: “Well, perhaps so,” Kostya agreed, entirely vanquished. “But you didn’t say so before. So how could I tell?”
11: “Come, kiddies,” said Kolya, stepping into the room. “You’re terrible people, I see.”
12: “And Perezvon with you!” grinned Kostya, and began snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.
13: “I am in a difficulty, kids,” Krassotkin began solemnly, “and you must help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she has not turned up till now, that’s certain. I must go out. Will you let me go?”
14: The children looked anxiously at one another. Their smiling faces showed signs of uneasiness, but they did not yet fully grasp what was expected of them.
15: “You won’t be naughty while I am gone? You won’t climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won’t be frightened alone and cry?”
16: A look of profound despondency came into the children’s faces.
17: “And I could show you something as a reward, a little copper cannon which can be fired with real gunpowder.”
18: The children’s faces instantly brightened. “Show us the cannon,” said Kostya, beaming all over.
20: Krassotkin put his hand in his satchel, and pulling out a little bronze cannon stood it on the table.
21: “Ah, you are bound to ask that! Look, it’s on wheels.” He rolled the toy on along the table. “And it can be fired off, too. It can be loaded with shot and fired off.”
23: “It can kill anyone; you’ve only got to aim at anybody,” and Krassotkin explained where the powder had to be put, where the shot should be rolled in, showing a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them that it kicked when it was fired. The children listened with intense interest. What particularly struck their imagination was that the cannon kicked.
24: “And have you got any powder?” Nastya inquired.
26: “Show us the powder, too,” she drawled with a smile of entreaty.
27: Krassotkin dived again into his satchel and pulled out a small flask containing a little real gunpowder. He had some shot, too, in a screw of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into the palm of his hand.
28: “One has to be careful there’s no fire about, or it would blow up and kill us all,” Krassotkin warned them sensationally.
29: The children gazed at the powder with an awestricken alarm that only intensified their enjoyment. But Kostya liked the shot better.
30: “And does the shot burn?” he inquired.
32: “Give me a little shot,” he asked in an imploring voice.
33: “I’ll give you a little shot; here, take it, but don’t show it to your mother till I come back, or she’ll be sure to think it’s gunpowder, and will die of fright and give you a thrashing.”
34: “Mother never does whip us,” Nastya observed at once.
35: “I know, I only said it to finish the sentence. And don’t you ever deceive your mother except just this once, until I come back. And so, kiddies, can I go out? You won’t be frightened and cry when I’m gone?”
36: “We sha—all cry,” drawled Kostya, on the verge of tears already.
37: “We shall cry, we shall be sure to cry,” Nastya chimed in with timid haste.
38: “Oh, children, children, how fraught with peril are your years! There’s no help for it, chickens, I shall have to stay with you I don’t know how long. And time is passing, time is passing, oogh!”
39: “Tell Perezvon to pretend to be dead!” Kostya begged.
40: “There’s no help for it, we must have recourse to Perezvon. Ici, Perezvon.” And Kolya began giving orders to the dog, who performed all his tricks. He was a rough-haired dog, of medium size, with a coat of a sort of lilac-gray color. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, lay on his back with his paws in the air, rigid as though he were dead. While this last performance was going on, the door opened and Agafya, Madame Krassotkin’s servant, a stout woman of forty, marked with smallpox, appeared in the doorway. She had come back from market and had a bag full of provisions in her hand. Holding up the bag of provisions in her left hand she stood still to watch the dog. Though Kolya had been so anxious for her return, he did not cut short the performance, and after keeping Perezvon dead for the usual time, at last he whistled to him. The dog jumped up and began bounding about in his joy at having done his duty.
41: “Only think, a dog!” Agafya observed sententiously.
42: “Why are you late, female?” asked Krassotkin sternly.
43: “Female, indeed! Go on with you, you brat.”
45: “Yes, a brat. What is it to you if I’m late; if I’m late, you may be sure I have good reason,” muttered Agafya, busying herself about the stove, without a trace of anger or displeasure in her voice. She seemed quite pleased, in fact, to enjoy a skirmish with her merry young master.
46: “Listen, you frivolous young woman,” Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, “can you swear by all you hold sacred in the world and something else besides, that you will watch vigilantly over the kids in my absence? I am going out.”
47: “And what am I going to swear for?” laughed Agafya. “I shall look after them without that.”
48: “No, you must swear on your eternal salvation. Else I shan’t go.”
49: “Well, don’t then. What does it matter to me? It’s cold out; stay at home.”
50: “Kids,” Kolya turned to the children, “this woman will stay with you till I come back or till your mother comes, for she ought to have been back long ago. She will give you some lunch, too. You’ll give them something, Agafya, won’t you?”
52: “Goodbye, chickens, I go with my heart at rest. And you, granny,” he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, “I hope you’ll spare their tender years and not tell them any of your old woman’s nonsense about Katerina. Ici, Perezvon!”
53: “Get along with you!” retorted Agafya, really angry this time. “Ridiculous boy! You want a whipping for saying such things, that’s what you want!”
